young.html: Blaise Pascal was a great French mathematician who invented one of the first calculating machines. Later in his short life he began a book to defend his Christian faith. He died before finishing it, at 39, and his friends found hundreds of notes on slips of paper. They printed them as Pensées, which means “Thoughts.”

Some of Pascal's thoughts are about how small we are. Compared with the stars we are tiny, and compared with the tiniest things we are huge. We are somewhere in the middle, between two endless distances. That made Pascal wonder about our place in the universe.

But Pascal also said we have something wonderful. He compared a person to a reed, a thin plant that bends in the wind and breaks easily. We are as weak as a reed, he said, but we are a thinking reed. The universe is huge, but it doesn't know anything. We can know and wonder.

Thinking reed. Find a blade of grass or a reed and look at how easily it bends. Then lie down outside (or look at a picture of the night sky) and think about how big the universe is. Talk about Pascal's idea: what can a thinking person do that a star cannot?
Pascal also wrote: “The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.” He meant that we know some things, like who we love, in a way that is different from proving them like math.

full.html: Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) was a mathematician and physicist (see his scientific rung) and the author of the Provincial Letters. From the late 1650s he gathered notes for an apology, in the old sense of a reasoned defense, of the Christian religion, aimed at people who did not believe or did not care. He died before writing it. The notes, nearly a thousand of them, were first printed in 1670. Editors have arranged them in different orders ever since; the numbers here are those of the English translation by W. F. Trotter.

Pascal describes human beings as a mixture of greatness and misery. We stand between two infinities, the infinitely large and the infinitely small, and can know neither end. We fill our days with diversions (games, hunting, business, conversation) so as not to think about our condition; he says much of human trouble comes from being unable to sit quietly in a room. Yet thought gives us dignity:

full.text:
Man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature; but he is a thinking reed. The entire universe need not arm itself to crush him. A vapour, a drop of water suffices to kill him. But, if the universe were to crush him, man would still be more noble than that which killed him, because he knows that he dies and the advantage which the universe has over him; the universe knows nothing of this.

All our dignity consists, then, in thought. By it we must elevate ourselves, and not by space and time which we cannot fill. Let us endeavour, then, to think well; this is the principle of morality.
full.author: Blaise Pascal
full.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 48, P. F. Collier & Son

full.html: The best-known note is the wager (233). Pascal says reason cannot settle whether God exists, yet we cannot avoid choosing, since not choosing is itself a choice: “you are embarked.” So he asks the reader to weigh the bet like a mathematician who studies games of chance. Betting that God is risks a finite life; it may gain an infinite happiness. Not betting gains, at most, finite pleasures.

full.text: Let us weigh the gain and the loss in wagering that God is. Let us estimate these two chances. If you gain, you gain all; if you lose, you lose nothing. Wager, then, without hesitation that He is.
full.author: Blaise Pascal
full.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 48, P. F. Collier & Son

full.name: gb-wager
full.cap: The wager set out as Pascal frames it, as a bet with an expected value. Try a finite reward to see why the infinite one decides the argument for him.

full.title: Expected value, the tool behind the wager
full.q: A game costs 2 points to play. With chance 1/10 you win 50 points; otherwise you win nothing. Is playing a good bet on average?
steps: The expected value is positive, so on average playing is the better choice.
Pascal's move: if the prize is infinite, then any chance above zero, times infinity, outweighs any finite cost.
full.a: Yes: an expected gain of 3 points.

full.html: Pascal adds that someone who is persuaded but still cannot believe should act as believers do, so that habit can quiet the passions that stand in the way. The wager is meant for a particular reader at a particular moment, not as the whole of his case.

full.text: The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know. We feel it in a thousand things.
full.author: Blaise Pascal
full.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 48, P. F. Collier & Son

full.html: By “heart” Pascal means a direct kind of knowing, not just feelings. We know first principles, such as that there is space, time and number, by the heart; reason then builds proofs on them. In the same way, he holds, faith is given to the heart. Elsewhere he contrasts the mathematical mind, which reasons from a few clear principles, with the intuitive mind, which sees many fine points at once.

Reading the wager as Pascal's main proof of God. He thought proofs of God from nature persuade few people, and he spends far more of the Pensées on the human condition and on the history and figures of the Bible.

deep.html: The wager has been debated for over three centuries. Critics ask which God to bet on, since many religions make claims (the “many gods” objection); whether belief can be chosen at all; and whether a God would reward belief adopted for gain. Voltaire, in his Philosophical Letters (1734), objected to Pascal's gloomy picture of human nature and to the wager itself. Pascal's defenders answer that the wager was written for a reader already weighing Christianity, and that its real aim is to show that indifference is not a reasonable position. These are Pascal's arguments and his critics' arguments; the lesson takes no side on the question itself.

The wager is one of the first uses of what is now called decision theory: choosing well when outcomes are uncertain by weighing their values and chances, an idea that grew out of Pascal's own work with Fermat on games of chance. His portrait of restless, distracted human beings has been taken up by religious and non-religious writers alike, including Kierkegaard and Dostoevsky in the next century.

items: Is it possible to decide to believe something?
Pascal says people stay busy so they don't have to think. Is that true today?
Are there things we know “by the heart” that we cannot prove?

questions: Pascal says we are weak like a reed but great because we think. What makes a person great, in your view?
Why do you think people keep busy instead of sitting quietly? Try sitting quietly for five minutes and talk about how it felt.
What do you know “by the heart” rather than by proof?
Pascal says not choosing is still a choice. Can you think of an example in everyday life?
What do you think of the wager as an argument? What would you ask Pascal about it?
care: The Pensées defend the Christian faith. This lesson presents Pascal's arguments as his own, gives the main objections fairly, and takes no side.
